title: Easy exam 15
about: Ten single-choice questions on the basics: job numbers, systemd targets, appending, env and printenv, grep options, crontab, wc, shift, ls -d and what a shell is.

questions.title: Bringing a job back
questions.text: `jobs` shows two stopped jobs, `[1]` and `[2]`. Which command brings job number 2 to the foreground?

options.why: `%2` names job number 2, and `fg` makes it the foreground job again.
It resumes job 2, but in the background.

options.t: `jobs %2`
options.why: It only lists the job; it does not change its state.

options.t: `kill %2`
options.why: It sends `SIGTERM` to job 2, which ends it.

options.t: The name of the target that the system reaches by default at boot, such as `graphical.target` or `multi-user.target`.
options.why: A target groups units, as the old runlevels did.

options.t: The number of the default runlevel, from 0 to 6.
options.why: `systemd` uses named targets; the numbers survive only as aliases.

options.t: The kernel that GRUB loads by default.
options.why: That is a GRUB setting, not a systemd one.

options.t: The list of the units that failed during the last boot.
options.why: Failed units are listed with `systemctl --failed`.

questions.title: Appending to a missing file
questions.text: `log.txt` does not exist. What does `echo hi >> log.txt` do?

options.t: It creates `log.txt` with the line `hi`.
options.why: `>>` appends and creates the file when it is missing.

options.t: It fails with "No such file or directory".
options.why: Redirections create the file; they do not need it to exist.

options.t: It does nothing, because there is no content to append to.
options.why: There is always something to append to: an empty file is created first.

options.t: It creates `log.txt` empty and prints `hi` on the screen.
options.why: The output of `echo` goes into the file, not to the screen.

questions.title: Variables that children see
questions.text: After `x=1; export y=2`, which statement about `printenv` is FALSE?

options.t: `printenv y` prints `2`.
options.why: True: `y` is exported, so it is in the environment.

options.t: `env` lists the exported variables, `y` among them.
options.why: True: `env` prints the environment of the shell.

options.t: A program started from this shell can read `y`.
options.why: True: exported variables are inherited by the child processes.

options.t: `printenv x` prints `1`, because every variable of the shell is shown by `printenv`.
options.why: False: `x` was not exported, so it is not part of the environment and `printenv x` prints nothing.

questions.title: The options of grep
questions.text: Which statement about the options of `grep` is FALSE?

options.t: `grep -i` ignores the difference between upper and lower case.
options.why: True.

options.t: `grep -v` prints the lines that do not match.
options.why: True: it inverts the selection.

options.t: `grep -n` puts the line number in front of every line it prints.
options.why: True.

options.t: `grep -c` prints the matching lines and, at the end, how many there were.
options.why: False: `-c` prints only the number of matching lines, not the lines themselves.

options.t: It lists the scheduled jobs in the crontab of the current user.
options.why: `-e` edits it and `-r` removes it.

options.t: It opens the crontab of the current user in an editor.
options.why: That is `crontab -e`.

options.t: It deletes all the jobs of the current user.
options.why: That is `crontab -r`.

options.t: It lists the jobs of all the users of the system.
options.why: Each user has a separate crontab; `-l` shows only your own.

options.t: `wc -m` counts characters and `wc -c` counts bytes.
options.why: For the line `é` the output of `wc -c` is 3 (two bytes plus the newline) and that of `wc -m` is 2.

options.t: `wc -l` counts the words and `wc -w` counts the lines.
options.why: `-l` counts lines; words are counted with `-w`.

options.t: `wc -w` counts the lines.
options.why: `-w` counts words.

options.t: `wc` with no option prints only the number of lines.
options.why: It prints lines, words and bytes, in that order.

questions.title: The shift command
questions.text: What does `shift` do in a script?

options.t: It discards `$1` and moves the rest down: `$2` becomes `$1`.
options.why: It is used to process the arguments one by one in a loop.

options.t: It moves the cursor to the next line of the script.
options.why: `shift` is not about the script text.

options.t: It shifts the content of a variable one character to the left, dropping the first.
options.why: It works on the positional parameters, not on strings.

options.t: It adds the first argument to the end of the list.
options.why: The first argument is discarded, not rotated.

questions.title: Listing a directory itself
questions.text: `dd` is a directory with a file inside. What does `ls -ld dd` print?

options.t: One line in long format that describes the directory `dd` itself.
options.why: `-d` lists the directory instead of its content.

options.t: The long listing of the files inside `dd`.
options.why: That is `ls -l dd`.

options.t: The inode number of `dd`.
options.why: That is `ls -i`.

options.t: The files inside `dd` and all its subdirectories.
options.why: That is `ls -R dd`.

questions.title: What a shell is
questions.text: What is the shell, in an operating system like Linux? Choose the TRUE statement.

options.t: It is a program that reads the lines you type, interprets them and runs the commands.
options.why: It is a normal program that runs on top of the kernel; bash is one of several shells.

options.t: It is the part of the kernel that manages the files.
options.why: The shell is an ordinary user-space program, not part of the kernel.

options.t: It is the only program that can start other programs.
options.why: Any program can start other programs; the shell does it for the user.

options.t: It is the program that the firmware starts first when the computer is switched on.
options.why: The firmware starts a boot loader, which loads the kernel; the shell comes much later.
